content_html:
Look at the gif below. It shows a proof-of-concept implementation of collaborative undo-redo, including "history mode undo", conflict handling, and async operations. In the process of designing and implementing it, I found myself digging down rabbit holes, questioning my own assumptions, and reading academic papers. In this post, I will share my learnings. The source code is available online.


Play with the live app

Context and motivation

Undo-redo is a staple of software systems, a feature so ubiquitous that users just assume apps would have it. As users, we absolutely love it because:

  1. It saves us when we make mistakes (e.g. delete or move something unintentionally).
  2. It encourages us to experiment and learn by doing (let's try clicking that button and see what happens; worst case we'll undo).
  3. Together with redo (which is, in fact, an undo of the undo), it allows us to back-track and iterate at zero cost.
  4. Both undo and redo (when implemented correctly, more on that later) are non-destructive operations (!), giving us a sense of safety and comfort.

As developers, however, implementing a robust undo-redo system is a non-trivial undertaking, with implications that penetrate every part of the app. In my previous post, I listed undo/redo as one of the hard problems in web development, so naturally I wanted to see what it would take to add this feature to my little collaborative todo-mvc toy app. I approached it with respect because I had evidence of its tricky nature:

  1. In a previous role, I witnessed a peer team struggling to add undo/redo to a WYSIWYG editor. Although I wasn't involved at the technical level, I was aware of some of the pain and challenges they faced, saw how long it took, and noticed how many bugs they had.
  2. When searching for undo-redo libraries, I couldn't find any that supported the multiplayer use-case. Even the library from the company that made Replicache didn't.
  3. As a user, I can't think of a single collaborative app that implements undo/redo in a way that feels right (if you know any, please leave a comment). It's also very noticeable in its absence in some major, popular apps. Is it because it was to hard to implement?
  4. When googling for information about undo-redo, I found (and eventually read) multiple academic papers and master's theses on the subject (e.g., this) . They don't write those about straightforward concepts, do they?
  5. I also found blog-posts from big players in the field, specifically one from Liveblocks and a short discussion about undo/redo in a post by Figma. I later learned that Figma's UX around undo/redo leaves a lot to be desired, which shows that identifying the problems is easier than coming up with good solutions.

Undo/ redo is a strange beast

I always knew that undo/redo is a deeply "strange" feature, but it was only when I started thinking about implementing it myself that some of its weirder aspects became more salient:

  1. We all do this: Undo, undo, undo... (repeat N times); copy something; redo, redo, redo (repeat N times); paste.
  2. And we get annoyed by this: Undo, undo, type a character, realise you can't redo anymore. (Does a disabled "redo" button mean some of the editing-history is lost forever? Spoiler alert: It depends on the implementation, as we'll see in the next section).
  3. And get anxious over this: Closed the window? Bye bye undo history. Opened the app on another device or tab to keep editing from where you left off? No undo history for you (hopefully the original tab is still open somewhere).
  4. And what happens if the original tab is still open, you edit on another tab, and then go back to the original tab and hit undo? Would that unintentionally corrupt the state?
  5. And when working with others on a collaborative whiteboard (e.g., Figma) or similar apps, did you notice how everyone carefully stay away of other people's way and stick to their own "territory"? What if two of them edited the same entity but not at the same time and one of them hits undo?

Points 1 and 2 are intentional design decisions that make undo/redo the feature we know and love. It sacrifices flexibility for speed and simplicity.
Points 3-5 are very sus and require a deeper look.

Modelling a branching state-graph

Let's dive into that second point first: What actually happens when you undo a few times, make a change and see your redo button disabled? The answer is: it depends. I'll explain.

State changes in a system can be represented as a graph. Undo allows us to traverse the graph "backwards in time," and redo allows us to trace our steps back (so "forwards in time") to the present.

Imagine we have the following sequence of operations on an element:

  1. Edit "" -> "Hello".
  2. Edit "Hello" -> "Hello World".
  3. Undo (the state becomes "Hello" again)
  4. Edit "Hello" -> "Hello Friend"

We can build a graph in which each unique state is represented by a node (like a state machine), as follows:

In this model, step 4 creates a new branch in the graph, and we lose our ability to return to the "Hello World" state. Going backwards from "Hello Friend," which is the present state, leads to "Hello" and then to "". Going forwards from there using "redo" takes us to "Hello" and then to "Hello Friend." That's because while there is always a single path backwards from any state to the initial state, there can be multiple paths forward but "redo" can only follow a single path - the path that leads to the "present" state.

Many systems follow this model, for example: Google Slides as you can see below:

This way of implementing undo/redo leads to increased user anxiety (== bad user experience) because after I undo, I need to be super careful or else I'd lose the ability to restore some states. The browser's "back" and "forward" buttons, which are basically undo/redo for the URL bar, behave this way as well.

But wait, this is not the only way! We can do better (this is where reading academic papers pays off).

What if we built our graph such that every node represented a point in time rather than a state? Time is linear (no branching unless you live in the multiverse) and always moves forward. This approach would represent the same sequence of operations like so:

Now we can never lose any change we've made in the past. Going backwards from "Hello Friend" takes us through every change we've ever made, as shown below.

This flavour of undo is called "History Undo" (see page 4 in this excellent academic paper). It was first introduced by Emacs. It leads to a much better user experience and feels very intuitive to use.

Notice that in both cases the "redo" button gets disabled when the user edits "Hello" to "Hello Friend" (which makes sense if you remember that redo is undo of undo). The difference is in how undo behaves after that point (and as a result, any subsequent "redo").

I implemented both modes in my proof of concept. "History undo" mode is enabled by default.
If you want to get into the nitty-gritty have a look at the source code.

The question of scope

An important property of a good undo-redo implementation is that it operates in the correct scope. In most applications, the expectation is for the undo-manager's scope to be the entire session. As I continuously hit "undo," I expect all the actions I took in the session to be rolled back. If I close the session, I expect to my undo stack to be lost.
If the scope is smaller than the whole session, it can be disorienting for users. For example, if your text-editor has a separate undo stack from the rest of the app, people will call you out on Twitter:

In web applications or desktop applications that supports multiple tabs (e.g., VSCode), a session equals a single tab.

The expectations I described above carry over from single-user to collaborative, multi-user applications. Users expect to only be able to undo/redo their own actions. Users don't seem to expect the undo/redo stack to exceed session scope e.g. be shared between multiple tabs or multiple devices (on which they have the app running). I wonder if it's just because no app has done that yet and once someone does, it would become the new norm. Wouldn't it be great to have your history available on all your devices?

In my implementation I remained within session-scope, like all standard implementations. I did it because it was the easier and quicker option. I might try to extend it to user-scope in future iterations. I am sure it will present interesting technical challenges.

Memento vs. Command pattern

One of the first resources I stumbled upon when I was doing my research was an article in the official Redux docs, explaining how to implement generic undo/redo using the Memento pattern. The idea is so simple: Just save a copy of the state every time it changes and store these state copies as "past" (array), "present" and "future" (array). Whenever you want to undo, push the present state into the "future" array, pop the head of the "past" array and make it the new present, the app re-renders, voilà. No need for app-specific logic, whatever your state shape is - it just works. It sounds so alluring, so beautiful and elegant - there is only one tiny problem: it doesn't work for anything besides the simplest of apps.

Here is why:

  1. It doesn't deal with side-effects. Undoing and redoing actions tends to involve much more than state changes on the frontend. Apps need to create or cleanup remote resources, call APIs and do all the stuff that real apps do. These side-effects and the logic for addressing them are specific, and need to be handled on a case by case basis by the app. In other words, transition between states involves more than just replacing one state object with another.
  2. The idea of replacing the state object wholesale is totally incompatible with simultaneous, collaborative editing. It leads to users constantly erasing each other's changes even if they are modifying different parts of the state.
  3. Even in React apps that use Redux, not all the state is managed by the central store. There is a bunch of local state in the components. Don't we want the undo/redo manager to be able to account for local component state as well?

Sadly, due to of all of the above, the Memento pattern is off the table. This leave us with the much less plug-and-play Command pattern. Instead of storing states we store commands and reverse-commands and execute them whenever we need to roll the state back or forward. "Commands" is just a fancy name for functions that modify state, e.g. "() => markTodoComplete(id, true)" and its reverse "() => markTodoComplete(id, false)".

The command pattern allows us to update the state granularly with less collisions. It allows us to apply arbitrary logic and deal with side effects, and it doesn't know or care about the application state or where it lives. These advantages come at a cost: For every action our app can perform, we now need to implement a reverse-action, and register both with the undo manager. But wait, there's more...

We can still have conflicts, can't we?

Multiple users making changes to the same "document" at the same time means that conflicts can and will occur. Having undo-redo thrown into the mix increases the likelihood of conflicts by introducing the possibility of unintentional and hidden conflicts. When real-time editing, users usually try to stay out of each other's way but the dimension of time makes that more tricky. If I edited a place at an earlier time, and later someone made changes on top of my changes, what's gonna happen if I casually "undo" ten times? I can unintentionally cause someone else to lose work. This can also happen via indirect conflicts - for example: user A creates an item, user B edits the item, user A clicks undo - deleting the item and deleting user B's work as a result (again, without intending or even realising it).
This sounds bad, right? The whole point of undo/redo is to allow users to experiment and time-travel safely, without worrying about accidentally corrupting the system's state.

Sync engines, like Replicache (which our little todo app uses), have the ability to deal with "realtime" conflicts between clients via an authoritative server that can reject and revert changes. However, we don't want the user experience errors due to rejected undo operations, or have nothing happen because the element they are trying to modify no longer exists. See it happening in Figma in the gif below (taken from here). Notice how some undo operations do nothing and the user needs to keep undoing to drain all the bad operations from the undo-stack. That's poor UX. We need to come up with an elegant way to deal with these situations.

Can we simply ignore conflicts?

Some smart people don't think that conflicts are a big deal in multiplayer systems. Adam Wiggins (co-founder of Heroku) for example, dismissed it in this part of his recent talk (not in the context of undo/redo but as a general concern). He was later challenged about it by a question from the audience at this timestamp but stood his ground. To summarise his reasoning: Users stay out of each others' way - it's a social thing (true). Also, when conflicts do occur, users are smart enough to realise what happened and fix it themselves, no big deal. He does note that this is true for the app he's creating (Muse), but might not apply in all cases.

I have to respectfully disagree. It's cool that users find creative ways to work with broken systems, but we can't use that as an excuse for building sub-par apps. We can and should do better for our users.

Dealing with conflicts - undo-manager perspective (in theory)

So, how can we deal with these nasty conflicts?
This paper lays down a solid foundation. I'll do my best to summarise its main ideas for you. The paper discusses the problem of "undoing actions in collaborative systems" in the context of a distributed text editor called DistEdit. It suggests that the undo-manager takes a "Conflict(A,B)" callback from the app, with the following spec (see section 4.2.1):

The Conflict(A, B) function supplied by the application must return true if the adjacent operations A and B performed in sequence cannot be reordered, and false otherwise . The importance of the notion of conflict is that it imposes an ordering on operations A and B. If Conflict(A, B) is true, then the order of operations A and B cannot, in general, be changed without affecting the results. Furthermore, in general, operation A cannot be undone, unless the following operation B is undone

The paper then offers an insight about the users' intentions (see section 5 "Selective Undo Algorithms"):

If an operation A is undone, we assume that users want their document to go to a state that it would have gone to if operation A had never been performed, but all other operations had been performed

To achieve this, the proposed algorithm first rolls back everything that came after the operation we want to undo, makes a backup copy of the "future" stack, and tries to preform the undo by "bubbling" the operation we are trying to get rid off up the stack, kinda like bubble sort. In each step it checks whether the operation we want to undo (A) has conflict with the next adjacent operation (B). If not, they can be swapped, and we can executed a "transposed" version of B without executing A.
This "transpose(A,B)" function, that the app needs to provide, makes sense in the context of text editing, where the cursor position, for example, could be different if operation A never happened. The algorithm keeps working its way up the stack until it either reaches the top (success) or hits a conflict. If it hits a conflict, it tries to get rid of it by checking whether the "future" has the reverse operation; if yes, both can be safely removed. If the conflict cannot be removed, the algorithm determines that the operation cannot be undone (failure). When that happens, the paper offers two options (see section 8.1.4):

  1. Show the conflicts to the user and ask them to resolve.
  2. Tell the user about the conflict, ignore that undo operation, and allow the user to undo older operations.

While I like the general idea, I had some issues with this algorithm:

  1. For a general-purpose undo-manager, outside of collaborative text editing (which most apps use CRDTs for nowadays), it seemed excessive to expect the app to provide transpose functions, which must satisfy five mathematical properties (see section 4.2.2 in the paper).
  2. I don't want users to be able try to undo something and end up failing. I want to detect the conflicts ahead of time - for better UX.
  3. While I think it makes sense to skip bad operations, I am not sure that it's a good idea to ask the user to do something about it. If we wanted that we should have implemented features like version-history or version-control rather than undo/redo. Keeping the user informed is, generally speaking, a good idea, but we should aspire to do it in a non-disruptive manner.

Dealing with conflicts - undo-manager perspective (in practice)

With all this in mind, I ended up with the following implementation:
The undo-manager allows each entry (action) to have the attributes 'scopeName', 'hasUndoConflict', and 'hasRedoConflict'. Unlike the "Conflict(A,B)" function from the paper, which takes two adjacent operations, my functions check whether a single undo or redo operation is valid in the context of the current state of the app.

The conflict checks run on the "head" of the undo and redo stacks after every operation, and remove conflicting entries (and everything else with the same scopeName) until a non-conflicting one is found. This way, the next action the user can take is always a non-conflicting one.
The undo-manager provides a way to tell the user when conflicting entries are removed (via a "change reason"), but in the demo app I used it in a very subtle way.

All in all, here is the type definition for a single undo-redo entry:

export type UndoEntry = {
    operation: () => void;
    reverseOperation: () => void;
    hasUndoConflict?: () => boolean | Promise<boolean>;
    hasRedoConflict?: () => boolean | Promise<boolean>;
    // determines what gets removed when there are conflicts
    scopeName: string;
    // will be returned from subscribeToCanUndoRedoChange so you can display it in a tooltip next to the buttons (e.g "un-create item")
    description: string;
    reverseDescription: string;
};

For the full implementation details and how it is used, have a look at the code, for example here.

Dealing with conflicts - app perspective

So the undo-manager facilitates a way to deal with conflicts, but it's up to the app to provide the actual conflict-checking logic. How should it go about that? One useful concept is "ownership".

In a single-user app, there is no question about who owns the data - there is only one user, but what about a multi-user, collaborative app? We can think about it as follows: The last user who modified a piece of data (direct modification - not via undo or redo) owns it. The owner of a piece of data can safely undo/redo their changes to it without overriding someone else's changes.
For example, if I created a todo item and you modified its description, I shouldn't be able to undo the creation of that item, but I should still be able to undo anything else that I have in my undo stack. The granularity of the ownership is determined by the app. If I modified the text of an item and you then marked it as completed, it is probably okay for me to undo my change because I own the description and you own the completeness. If I later directly modify the completeness, I should be able to undo and redo that, and you shouldn't, because I took ownership over completeness.

The gif below shows a simple example: When the user on the right edits the text of the second item, the user on the left loses the ability to undo any edits to its text or its creation, but still has the ability to undo the creation of the first item (which they still own). A sharp-eyed viewer would notice that the undo icon on the left animates when the conflicting entries are removed (when the user on the right enters the text "nope!").

If you don't agree with the specific logic I applied here, that's okay - the logic is totally flexible. The important thing is that we have an undo-manager that makes this possible.

Getting the user experience right

In the gif above, did you notice that little tooltip (just a "title" attribute in this demo) that tells the user what's going to happen when they click undo/redo when they hover over the button? Did you notice how the buttons animate when there is a change in the undo/ redo stack? To achieve these, the undo-manager provides a simple pub-sub service so that the consumer can stay up to speed.

Dealing with asynchrony

The undo-manager has to be able to handle both synchronous and asynchronous operations because all the Replicache calls are async, and in other real-world systems, any call to the backend or external APIs would be async as well. The challenge with async operations is that they can complete in different order to how they start (depending on how long it takes each promise to resolve) and query the system while it's "between states." For example, an operation starts running, and then while it's awaiting something, an "undo" or a conflict check starts running and make their own changes. To deal with that, I introduced a simple module that executes the async operations serially using a queue.

Places where my demo implementation falls short

If you read my previous post, you’d know that I was thoroughly impressed by Replicache. That's still true, but I have hit some walls (missing features) when adding undo-redo to the app. It’s important to note that the undo-manager itself is generic (agnostic about Replicache) but does pose some expectations that Replicache fails to meet (all seem fixable). Here are the main challenges I faced:

  1. Distinguishing between self inflicted and external updates: When Replicache informs the app about incoming changes from the server, it doesn’t indicate whether these changes originate in the current session or in some other session (external). We’d like to initiate conflict checks when there are incoming external changes, otherwise they already ran when taking the action (before sending it to the server), but how? I ended up adding some app-specific logic to detect that. Ideally, once Replicache exposes that info (relevant issue here), this kind of hack won’t be needed.
  2. Failure of an optimistic update: Replicache uses optimistic updates, meaning that the server can reject operations or return with a different than expected outcome. When that happens, the state is rolled back and adjusted to reflect the server state. When Replicache does that, it doesn’t notify the app, it comes in as any other state update. That makes it hard to adjust the undo stack, which still contains the original updates that the server just rejected. I could have probably worked around it but opted to leave it unimplemented in this POC. Ideally, Replicache would expose that information in the future.
  3. Coming back from offline mode: If you go offline, you can do anything you want (including undo/redo) and when you come back online your changes will be pushed to the server and override anything other users did while you were offline. This problem is not specific to undo/redo but a result of the Last Write Wins conflict-resolution strategy that my app uses. In theory, this could be mitigated by adding more sophisticated logic to the server’s mutators, but that would require more research to get right (maybe a good subject for another post).
  4. Lack of Integration with CRDT-based undo: Supporting embedded text editors in a way that is user friendly remains a challenge (I haven't attempted it yet, another idea for a future post :)).

Closing thoughts

We've covered a lot of ground in this post. While I spent most of it discussing different aspects of the undo-manager, in reality the majority of my time and effort were spent on carefully thinking through and implementing the app's reverse-operations and conflict-checking logic.

In some cases, I had to refactor the app and break down operations to make them undo/redo-friendly. For example, “completeAllItems” couldn’t remain a simple loop that calls “updateItem” with each item-id; it had to become its own thing with its own reverse logic (because maybe another user added or edited items). Some changes to the backend were required as well, such as adding an “un-delete” operation, which is different from “create” because it preserves the original sort position of the item. The database schema changed because I needed to add an "updatedBy" field on each todo, and these are just some examples. Testing is another task that grows considerably when your app has undo-redo.

In other words, undo-redo is one of those features that make every other feature in your app more complicated and time-consuming to implement and maintain. Is it worth it? I think the answer is a resounding yes for productivity apps and content-editors of any kind, but you need to know what you’re getting yourself into. It is definitely not for the faint of heart.

Thank you for reading. Feel free to leave a comment if you have any questions or insights.

Whenever you want to undo, push the present state into the "future" array, pop the head of the "past" array and make it the new present, the app re-renders, voilà. No need for app-specific logic, whatever your state shape is - it just works. It sounds so alluring, so beautiful and elegant - there is only one tiny problem: it doesn't work for anything besides the simplest of apps. Here is why: It doesn't deal with side-effects. Undoing and redoing actions tends to involve much more than state changes on the frontend. Apps need to create or cleanup remote resources, call APIs and do all the stuff that real apps do. These side-effects and the logic for addressing them are specific, and need to be handled on a case by case basis by the app. In other words, transition between states involves more than just replacing one state object with another. The idea of replacing the state object wholesale is totally incompatible with simultaneous, collaborative editing. It leads to users constantly erasing each other's changes even if they are modifying different parts of the state. Even in React apps that use Redux, not all the state is managed by the central store. There is a bunch of local state in the components. Don't we want the undo/redo manager to be able to account for local component state as well? Sadly, due to of all of the above, the Memento pattern is off the table. This leave us with the much less plug-and-play Command pattern. Instead of storing states we store commands and reverse-commands and execute them whenever we need to roll the state back or forward. "Commands" is just a fancy name for functions that modify state, e.g. "() => markTodoComplete(id, true)" and its reverse "() => markTodoComplete(id, false)". The command pattern allows us to update the state granularly with less collisions. It allows us to apply arbitrary logic and deal with side effects, and it doesn't know or care about the application state or where it lives. These advantages come at a cost: For every action our app can perform, we now need to implement a reverse-action, and register both with the undo manager. But wait, there's more... We can still have conflicts, can't we? Multiple users making changes to the same "document" at the same time means that conflicts can and will occur. Having undo-redo thrown into the mix increases the likelihood of conflicts by introducing the possibility of unintentional and hidden conflicts. When real-time editing, users usually try to stay out of each other's way but the dimension of time makes that more tricky. If I edited a place at an earlier time, and later someone made changes on top of my changes, what's gonna happen if I casually "undo" ten times? I can unintentionally cause someone else to lose work. This can also happen via indirect conflicts - for example: user A creates an item, user B edits the item, user A clicks undo - deleting the item and deleting user B's work as a result (again, without intending or even realising it). This sounds bad, right? The whole point of undo/redo is to allow users to experiment and time-travel safely, without worrying about accidentally corrupting the system's state. Sync engines, like Replicache (which our little todo app uses), have the ability to deal with "realtime" conflicts between clients via an authoritative server that can reject and revert changes. However, we don't want the user experience errors due to rejected undo operations, or have nothing happen because the element they are trying to modify no longer exists. See it happening in Figma in the gif below (taken from here). Notice how some undo operations do nothing and the user needs to keep undoing to drain all the bad operations from the undo-stack. That's poor UX. We need to come up with an elegant way to deal with these situations. Can we simply ignore conflicts? Some smart people don't think that conflicts are a big deal in multiplayer systems. Adam Wiggins (co-founder of Heroku) for example, dismissed it in this part of his recent talk (not in the context of undo/redo but as a general concern). He was later challenged about it by a question from the audience at this timestamp but stood his ground. To summarise his reasoning: Users stay out of each others' way - it's a social thing (true). Also, when conflicts do occur, users are smart enough to realise what happened and fix it themselves, no big deal. He does note that this is true for the app he's creating (Muse), but might not apply in all cases. I have to respectfully disagree. It's cool that users find creative ways to work with broken systems, but we can't use that as an excuse for building sub-par apps. We can and should do better for our users. Dealing with conflicts - undo-manager perspective (in theory) So, how can we deal with these nasty conflicts? This paper lays down a solid foundation. I'll do my best to summarise its main ideas for you. The paper discusses the problem of "undoing actions in collaborative systems" in the context of a distributed text editor called DistEdit. It suggests that the undo-manager takes a "Conflict(A,B)" callback from the app, with the following spec (see section 4.2.1): The Conflict(A, B) function supplied by the application must return true if the adjacent operations A and B performed in sequence cannot be reordered, and false otherwise . The importance of the notion of conflict is that it imposes an ordering on operations A and B. If Conflict(A, B) is true, then the order of operations A and B cannot, in general, be changed without affecting the results. Furthermore, in general, operation A cannot be undone, unless the following operation B is undone The paper then offers an insight about the users' intentions (see section 5 "Selective Undo Algorithms"): If an operation A is undone, we assume that users want their document to go to a state that it would have gone to if operation A had never been performed, but all other operations had been performed To achieve this, the proposed algorithm first rolls back everything that came after the operation we want to undo, makes a backup copy of the "future" stack, and tries to preform the undo by "bubbling" the operation we are trying to get rid off up the stack, kinda like bubble sort. In each step it checks whether the operation we want to undo (A) has conflict with the next adjacent operation (B). If not, they can be swapped, and we can executed a "transposed" version of B without executing A. This "transpose(A,B)" function, that the app needs to provide, makes sense in the context of text editing, where the cursor position, for example, could be different if operation A never happened. The algorithm keeps working its way up the stack until it either reaches the top (success) or hits a conflict. If it hits a conflict, it tries to get rid of it by checking whether the "future" has the reverse operation; if yes, both can be safely removed. If the conflict cannot be removed, the algorithm determines that the operation cannot be undone (failure). When that happens, the paper offers two options (see section 8.1.4): Show the conflicts to the user and ask them to resolve. Tell the user about the conflict, ignore that undo operation, and allow the user to undo older operations. While I like the general idea, I had some issues with this algorithm: For a general-purpose undo-manager, outside of collaborative text editing (which most apps use CRDTs for nowadays), it seemed excessive to expect the app to provide transpose functions, which must satisfy five mathematical properties (see section 4.2.2 in the paper). I don't want users to be able try to undo something and end up failing. I want to detect the conflicts ahead of time - for better UX. While I think it makes sense to skip bad operations, I am not sure that it's a good idea to ask the user to do something about it. If we wanted that we should have implemented features like version-history or version-control rather than undo/redo. Keeping the user informed is, generally speaking, a good idea, but we should aspire to do it in a non-disruptive manner. Dealing with conflicts - undo-manager perspective (in practice) With all this in mind, I ended up with the following implementation: The undo-manager allows each entry (action) to have the attributes 'scopeName', 'hasUndoConflict', and 'hasRedoConflict'. Unlike the "Conflict(A,B)" function from the paper, which takes two adjacent operations, my functions check whether a single undo or redo operation is valid in the context of the current state of the app. The conflict checks run on the "head" of the undo and redo stacks after every operation, and remove conflicting entries (and everything else with the same scopeName) until a non-conflicting one is found. This way, the next action the user can take is always a non-conflicting one. The undo-manager provides a way to tell the user when conflicting entries are removed (via a "change reason"), but in the demo app I used it in a very subtle way. All in all, here is the type definition for a single undo-redo entry: export type UndoEntry = { operation: () => void; reverseOperation: () => void; hasUndoConflict?: () => boolean | Promise<boolean>; hasRedoConflict?: () => boolean | Promise<boolean>; // determines what gets removed when there are conflicts scopeName: string; // will be returned from subscribeToCanUndoRedoChange so you can display it in a tooltip next to the buttons (e.g "un-create item") description: string; reverseDescription: string; }; Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode For the full implementation details and how it is used, have a look at the code, for example here. Dealing with conflicts - app perspective So the undo-manager facilitates a way to deal with conflicts, but it's up to the app to provide the actual conflict-checking logic. How should it go about that? One useful concept is "ownership". In a single-user app, there is no question about who owns the data - there is only one user, but what about a multi-user, collaborative app? We can think about it as follows: The last user who modified a piece of data (direct modification - not via undo or redo) owns it. The owner of a piece of data can safely undo/redo their changes to it without overriding someone else's changes. For example, if I created a todo item and you modified its description, I shouldn't be able to undo the creation of that item, but I should still be able to undo anything else that I have in my undo stack. The granularity of the ownership is determined by the app. If I modified the text of an item and you then marked it as completed, it is probably okay for me to undo my change because I own the description and you own the completeness. If I later directly modify the completeness, I should be able to undo and redo that, and you shouldn't, because I took ownership over completeness. The gif below shows a simple example: When the user on the right edits the text of the second item, the user on the left loses the ability to undo any edits to its text or its creation, but still has the ability to undo the creation of the first item (which they still own). A sharp-eyed viewer would notice that the undo icon on the left animates when the conflicting entries are removed (when the user on the right enters the text "nope!"). If you don't agree with the specific logic I applied here, that's okay - the logic is totally flexible. The important thing is that we have an undo-manager that makes this possible. Getting the user experience right In the gif above, did you notice that little tooltip (just a "title" attribute in this demo) that tells the user what's going to happen when they click undo/redo when they hover over the button? Did you notice how the buttons animate when there is a change in the undo/ redo stack? To achieve these, the undo-manager provides a simple pub-sub service so that the consumer can stay up to speed. Dealing with asynchrony The undo-manager has to be able to handle both synchronous and asynchronous operations because all the Replicache calls are async, and in other real-world systems, any call to the backend or external APIs would be async as well. The challenge with async operations is that they can complete in different order to how they start (depending on how long it takes each promise to resolve) and query the system while it's "between states." For example, an operation starts running, and then while it's awaiting something, an "undo" or a conflict check starts running and make their own changes. To deal with that, I introduced a simple module that executes the async operations serially using a queue. Places where my demo implementation falls short If you read my previous post, you’d know that I was thoroughly impressed by Replicache. That's still true, but I have hit some walls (missing features) when adding undo-redo to the app. It’s important to note that the undo-manager itself is generic (agnostic about Replicache) but does pose some expectations that Replicache fails to meet (all seem fixable). Here are the main challenges I faced: Distinguishing between self inflicted and external updates: When Replicache informs the app about incoming changes from the server, it doesn’t indicate whether these changes originate in the current session or in some other session (external). We’d like to initiate conflict checks when there are incoming external changes, otherwise they already ran when taking the action (before sending it to the server), but how? I ended up adding some app-specific logic to detect that. Ideally, once Replicache exposes that info (relevant issue here), this kind of hack won’t be needed. Failure of an optimistic update: Replicache uses optimistic updates, meaning that the server can reject operations or return with a different than expected outcome. When that happens, the state is rolled back and adjusted to reflect the server state. When Replicache does that, it doesn’t notify the app, it comes in as any other state update. That makes it hard to adjust the undo stack, which still contains the original updates that the server just rejected. I could have probably worked around it but opted to leave it unimplemented in this POC. Ideally, Replicache would expose that information in the future. Coming back from offline mode: If you go offline, you can do anything you want (including undo/redo) and when you come back online your changes will be pushed to the server and override anything other users did while you were offline. This problem is not specific to undo/redo but a result of the Last Write Wins conflict-resolution strategy that my app uses. In theory, this could be mitigated by adding more sophisticated logic to the server’s mutators, but that would require more research to get right (maybe a good subject for another post). Lack of Integration with CRDT-based undo: Supporting embedded text editors in a way that is user friendly remains a challenge (I haven't attempted it yet, another idea for a future post :)). Closing thoughts We've covered a lot of ground in this post. While I spent most of it discussing different aspects of the undo-manager, in reality the majority of my time and effort were spent on carefully thinking through and implementing the app's reverse-operations and conflict-checking logic. In some cases, I had to refactor the app and break down operations to make them undo/redo-friendly. For example, “completeAllItems” couldn’t remain a simple loop that calls “updateItem” with each item-id; it had to become its own thing with its own reverse logic (because maybe another user added or edited items). Some changes to the backend were required as well, such as adding an “un-delete” operation, which is different from “create” because it preserves the original sort position of the item. The database schema changed because I needed to add an "updatedBy" field on each todo, and these are just some examples. Testing is another task that grows considerably when your app has undo-redo. In other words, undo-redo is one of those features that make every other feature in your app more complicated and time-consuming to implement and maintain. Is it worth it? I think the answer is a resounding yes for productivity apps and content-editors of any kind, but you need to know what you’re getting yourself into. It is definitely not for the faint of heart. Thank you for reading. Feel free to leave a comment if you have any questions or insights.

blocks.html_en: One of the first resources I stumbled upon when I was doing my research was an article in the official Redux docs, explaining how to implement generic undo/redo using the Memento pattern. The idea is so simple: Just save a copy of the state every time it changes and store these state copies as "past" (array), "present" and "future" (array). Whenever you want to undo, push the present state into the "future" array, pop the head of the "past" array and make it the new present, the app re-renders, voilà. No need for app-specific logic, whatever your state shape is - it just works. It sounds so alluring, so beautiful and elegant - there is only one tiny problem: it doesn't work for anything besides the simplest of apps.

blocks.html_en: • It doesn't deal with side-effects. Undoing and redoing actions tends to involve much more than state changes on the frontend. Apps need to create or cleanup remote resources, call APIs and do all the stuff that real apps do. These side-effects and the logic for addressing them are specific, and need to be handled on a case by case basis by the app. In other words, transition between states involves more than just replacing one state object with another.

It allows us to apply arbitrary logic and deal with side effects, and it doesn't know or care about the application state or where it lives. These advantages come at a cost: For every action our app can perform, we now need to implement a reverse-action, and register both with the undo manager. But wait, there's more...

blocks.html_en: We can still have conflicts, can't we?

sentences.en: We can still have conflicts, can't we?
sentences.zh: 我们还是有矛盾的，不是吗？

blocks.html_en:
Multiple users making changes to the same "document" at the same time means that conflicts can and will occur. Having undo-redo thrown into the mix increases the likelihood of conflicts by introducing the possibility of unintentional and hidden conflicts. When real-time editing, users usually try to stay out of each other's way but the dimension of time makes that more tricky. If I edited a place at an earlier time, and later someone made changes on top of my changes, what's gonna happen if I casually "undo" ten times? I can unintentionally cause someone else to lose work. This can also happen via indirect conflicts - for example: user A creates an item, user B edits the item, user A clicks undo - deleting the item and deleting user B's work as a result (again, without intending or even realising it).
This sounds bad, right? The whole point of undo/redo is to allow users to experiment and time-travel safely, without worrying about accidentally corrupting the system's state.

blocks.html_en: So the undo-manager facilitates a way to deal with conflicts, but it's up to the app to provide the actual conflict-checking logic. How should it go about that? One useful concept is "ownership".

sentences.en: One useful concept is "ownership".

blocks.html_en:
In a single-user app, there is no question about who owns the data - there is only one user, but what about a multi-user, collaborative app? We can think about it as follows: The last user who modified a piece of data (direct modification - not via undo or redo) owns it. The owner of a piece of data can safely undo/redo their changes to it without overriding someone else's changes.
For example, if I created a todo item and you modified its description, I shouldn't be able to undo the creation of that item, but I should still be able to undo anything else that I have in my undo stack. The granularity of the ownership is determined by the app. If I modified the text of an item and you then marked it as completed, it is probably okay for me to undo my change because I own the description and you own the completeness. If I later directly modify the completeness, I should be able to undo and redo that, and you shouldn't, because I took ownership over completeness.

blocks.html_en: The undo-manager has to be able to handle both synchronous and asynchronous operations because all the Replicache calls are async, and in other real-world systems, any call to the backend or external APIs would be async as well. The challenge with async operations is that they can complete in different order to how they start (depending on how long it takes each promise to resolve) and query the system while it's "between states." For example, an operation starts running, and then while it's awaiting something, an "undo" or a conflict check starts running and make their own changes. To deal with that, I introduced a simple module that executes the async operations serially using a queue.

blocks.html_en: If you read my previous post, you’d know that I was thoroughly impressed by Replicache. That's still true, but I have hit some walls (missing features) when adding undo-redo to the app. It’s important to note that the undo-manager itself is generic (agnostic about Replicache) but does pose some expectations that Replicache fails to meet (all seem fixable). Here are the main challenges I faced:

sentences.en: Here are the main challenges I faced:
sentences.zh: 以下是我面临的主要挑战：

blocks.html_en: • Distinguishing between self inflicted and external updates: When Replicache informs the app about incoming changes from the server, it doesn’t indicate whether these changes originate in the current session or in some other session (external). We’d like to initiate conflict checks when there are incoming external changes, otherwise they already ran when taking the action (before sending it to the server), but how? I ended up adding some app-specific logic to detect that. Ideally, once Replicache exposes that info (relevant issue here), this kind of hack won’t be needed.

blocks.html_en: • Failure of an optimistic update: Replicache uses optimistic updates, meaning that the server can reject operations or return with a different than expected outcome. When that happens, the state is rolled back and adjusted to reflect the server state. When Replicache does that, it doesn’t notify the app, it comes in as any other state update. That makes it hard to adjust the undo stack, which still contains the original updates that the server just rejected. I could have probably worked around it but opted to leave it unimplemented in this POC. Ideally, Replicache would expose that information in the future.

In theory, this could be mitigated by adding more sophisticated logic to the server’s mutators, but that would require more research to get right (maybe a good subject for another post).

content_html_zh:
看看下面的动图。 它展示了协作撤消重做的概念验证实现，包括“历史模式撤消”、冲突处理和异步操作。 在设计和实现它的过程中，我发现自己在挖掘兔子洞，质疑自己的假设，并阅读学术论文。 在这篇文章中，我将分享我的学习成果。 源代码可在线获取。

使用实时应用程序进行游戏

背景和动机

撤消重做是软件系统的一个主要功能，这一功能如此普遍，以至于用户只是认为应用程序会拥有它。 作为用户，我们绝对喜欢它，因为：

  1. 当我们犯错误时（例如无意中删除或移动某些内容），它可以拯救我们。
  2. 它鼓励我们通过实践进行实验和学习（让我们尝试单击该按钮，看看会发生什么；最坏的情况我们将撤消）。
  3. 与重做（实际上是撤消的撤消）一起，它允许我们以零成本回溯和迭代。
  4. 撤消和重做（如果正确实现，稍后会详细介绍）都是非破坏性操作（！），给我们一种安全感和舒适感。

然而，作为开发人员，实现强大的撤消重做系统并非易事，其影响渗透到应用程序的每个部分。 在我的上一篇文章中，我将撤消/重做列为 Web 开发中的难题之一，因此我很自然地想看看如何将此功能添加到我的小型协作 todo-mvc 玩具应用程序中。 我怀着尊重的态度对待它，因为我有证据表明它的棘手本质：

  1. 在之前的角色中，我目睹了一个同行团队努力向所见即所得编辑器添加撤消/重做。 虽然我没有参与技术层面，但我知道他们面临的一些痛苦和挑战，看到了他们花了多长时间，并注意到他们有多少错误。
  2. 在搜索撤消重做库时，我找不到任何支持多人游戏用例的库。 即使是制作 Replicache 的公司的库也没有。
  3. 作为一名用户，我想不出有哪个协作应用程序能够以一种感觉正确的方式实现撤消/重做（如果您知道，请发表评论）。 它在一些主要流行应用程序中的缺失也非常引人注目。 是因为实施起来太难了吗？
  4. 当在谷歌上搜索有关撤消重做的信息时，我发现（并最终阅读）了多篇关于该主题的学术论文和硕士论文（例如，这个）。 他们不会写那些简单的概念，不是吗？
  5. 我还找到了该领域大玩家的博客文章，特别是来自 Liveblocks 的博文，以及 Figma 的一篇文章中关于撤消/重做的简短讨论。 后来我了解到 Figma 围绕撤消/重做的用户体验还有很多不足之处，这表明识别问题比提出好的解决方案更容易。

撤消/重做是一种奇怪的野兽

我一直都知道撤消/重做是一个非常“奇怪”的功能，但只有当我开始考虑自己实现它时，它的一些奇怪的方面才变得更加突出：

  1. 我们都会这样做：撤消，撤消，撤消...... （重复N次）；复制一些东西；重做，重做，重做（重复N次）；粘贴。
  2. 我们对此感到恼火：撤消，撤消，键入一个字符，意识到你无法再重做。 （禁用的“重做”按钮是否意味着某些编辑历史记录将永远丢失？ 剧透警告：这取决于实现，我们将在下一节中看到）。
  3. 并为此感到焦虑：关了窗户吗？ 再见撤消历史。 在其他设备或选项卡上打开应用程序以继续从上次中断的位置进行编辑？ 您没有撤消历史记录（希望原始选项卡仍然在某处打开）。
  4. 如果原始选项卡仍然打开，您在另一个选项卡上进行编辑，然后返回到原始选项卡并单击撤消，会发生什么情况？ 这会无意中腐蚀国家吗？
  5. 当与其他人在协作白板（例如Figma）或类似应用程序上工作时，您是否注意到每个人都小心翼翼地远离其他人的方式并坚持自己的“领地”？ 如果其中两个人不同时编辑同一个实体，并且其中一个人点击撤消怎么办？

第 1 点和第 2 点是有意的设计决策，使撤消/重做成为我们熟悉和喜爱的功能。 它牺牲了灵活性以换取速度和简单性。 第 3-5 点非常可疑，需要更深入地研究。

模拟分支状态图

让我们首先深入探讨第二点：当您撤消几次、进行更改并看到重做按钮被禁用时，实际上会发生什么？ 答案是：视情况而定。 我会解释一下。

系统中的状态变化可以用图形表示。 撤消允许我们“在时间上向后”遍历图表，而重做则允许我们回溯（因此“在时间上向前”）到现在的步骤。

想象一下我们对一个元素有以下操作序列：

  1. 编辑“”->“你好”。
  2. 编辑“Hello”->“Hello World”。
  3. 撤消（状态再次变为“Hello”）
  4. 编辑“你好”->“你好朋友”

我们可以构建一个图，其中每个唯一状态都由一个节点（如状态机）表示，如下所示：

在此模型中，第 4 步在图中创建了一个新分支，并且我们失去了返回“Hello World”状态的能力。 从当前状态“Hello Friend”向后返回到“Hello”，然后到“”。 从那里使用“重做”将我们带到“你好”，然后到“你好朋友”。 这是因为，虽然从任何状态到初始状态总是有一条向后路径，但可以有多个前进路径，但“重做”只能遵循一条路径 - 通向“当前”状态的路径。

范围问题

良好的撤消重做实现的一个重要属性是它在正确的范围内运行。 在大多数应用程序中，期望撤消管理器的范围是整个会话。 当我不断点击“撤消”时，我希望我在会话中执行的所有操作都会回滚。 如果我关闭会话，我预计我的撤消堆栈将会丢失。 如果范围小于整个会话，用户可能会感到迷惑。 例如，如果你的文本编辑器有一个与应用程序其余部分分开的撤消堆栈，人们会在 Twitter 上喊你：

在支持多个选项卡的 Web 应用程序或桌面应用程序（例如 VSCode）中，一个会话相当于一个选项卡。

我上面描述的期望从单用户应用程序延伸到协作、多用户应用程序。 用户期望只能撤消/重做自己的操作。 用户似乎并不期望撤消/重做堆栈超出会话范围，例如在多个选项卡或多个设备（运行应用程序的设备）之间共享。 我想知道这是否只是因为还没有应用程序做到这一点，一旦有人这样做，它就会成为新的规范。 如果您的历史记录可以在您的所有设备上查看，这不是很棒吗？

在我的实现中，我仍然在会话范围内，就像所有标准实现一样。 我这样做是因为这是更容易、更快捷的选择。 我可能会尝试在未来的迭代中将其扩展到用户范围。 我相信它将带来有趣的技术挑战。

备忘录与命令模式

我在进行研究时偶然发现的第一个资源是官方 Redux 文档中的一篇文章，解释了如何使用 Memento 模式实现通用撤消/重做。 这个想法很简单：只需在状态每次更改时保存一个副本，并将这些状态副本存储为“过去”（数组）、“现在”和“未来”（数组）。 每当您想要撤消时，将当前状态推入“未来”数组，弹出“过去”数组的头部并使其成为新的当前状态，应用程序重新渲染，瞧。 不需要特定于应用程序的逻辑，无论您的状态形状是什么 - 它都能正常工作。 它听起来如此诱人，如此美丽和优雅 - 只有一个小问题：除了最简单的应用程序之外，它不适用于任何其他应用程序。

原因如下：

  1. 它不涉及副作用。 撤消和重做操作往往不仅仅涉及前端的状态更改。 应用程序需要创建或清理远程资源、调用 API 并执行真实应用程序所做的所有操作。 这些副作用和解决它们的逻辑是特定的，需要由应用程序根据具体情况进行处理。 换句话说，状态之间的转换不仅仅涉及用一个状态对象替换另一个状态对象。
  2. 批量替换状态对象的想法与同时协作编辑完全不兼容。 它导致用户不断地擦除彼此的更改，即使他们正在修改状态的不同部分。
  3. 即使在使用 Redux 的 React 应用程序中，并非所有状态都由中央存储管理。 组件中有一堆本地状态。 难道我们不希望撤消/重做管理器也能够考虑本地组件状态吗？

遗憾的是，由于上述所有原因，Memento 模式已不再可行。 这给我们留下了更少的即插即用命令模式。 我们不存储状态，而是存储命令和反向命令，并在需要回滚或前进状态时执行它们。 “命令”只是修改状态的函数的一个奇特名称，例如“() => markTodoComplete(id, true)”及其相反的“() => markTodoComplete(id, false)”。

命令模式允许我们以更少的冲突精细地更新状态。 它允许我们应用任意逻辑并处理副作用，并且它不知道或关心应用程序状态或其所在位置。 这些优势是有代价的：对于我们的应用程序可以执行的每个操作，我们现在需要实现反向操作，并将两者注册到撤消管理器。 但是等等，还有更多……

我们还是有矛盾的，不是吗？

多个用户同时对同一“文档”进行更改意味着可能并且将会发生冲突。 将撤消和重做混合在一起会引入无意和隐藏冲突的可能性，从而增加了发生冲突的可能性。 在进行实时编辑时，用户通常会尽量避免妨碍彼此，但时间的维度使这变得更加棘手。 如果我之前编辑过一个地方，后来有人在我的修改之上进行了修改，那么如果我随便“撤消”十次会发生什么？ 我可能会无意中导致别人失业。 这也可能通过间接冲突发生 - 例如：用户 A 创建一个项目，用户 B 编辑该项目，用户 A 单击撤消 - 删除该项目并因此删除用户 B 的工作（同样，无意甚至没有意识到）。 这听起来很糟糕，对吧？ 撤消/重做的全部目的是允许用户安全地进行实验和时间旅行，而不必担心意外损坏系统状态。

同步引擎，如 Replicache（我们的小待办事项应用程序使用的），能够通过可以拒绝和恢复更改的权威服务器来处理客户端之间的“实时”冲突。 但是，我们不希望用户因撤消操作被拒绝而遇到错误，或者因为他们尝试修改的元素不再存在而没有发生任何事情。 在下面的 gif 中可以看到 Figma 中发生的情况（取自此处）。 请注意，某些撤消操作不执行任何操作，并且用户需要继续撤消以从撤消堆栈中排出所有不良操作。 这是糟糕的用户体验。 我们需要想出一种优雅的方法来处理这些情况。

我们能简单地忽略冲突吗？

一些聪明人认为冲突在多人游戏系统中并不是什么大问题。 例如，Adam Wiggins（Heroku 的联合创始人）在他最近演讲的这一部分中驳回了这一点（不是在撤消/重做的背景下，而是作为一个普遍关注的问题）。 随后，他在这个时间点受到了观众提出的质疑，但他坚持自己的立场。 总结一下他的推理：用户不妨碍彼此——这是一件社交事情（没错）。 此外，当冲突确实发生时，用户足够聪明，能够意识到发生了什么并自行修复，没什么大不了的。 他确实指出，这对于他正在创建的应用程序（Muse）来说是正确的，但可能并不适用于所有情况。

我必须恭敬地表示不同意。 用户找到创造性的方法来处理损坏的系统，这很酷，但我们不能以此为借口来构建低于标准的应用程序。 我们可以而且应该为我们的用户做得更好。

处理冲突——撤消管理者视角（理论上）

那么，我们该如何处理这些令人讨厌的冲突呢？ 本文奠定了坚实的基础。 我将尽力为您总结其主要思想。 该论文讨论了在名为 DistEdit 的分布式文本编辑器的上下文中“撤销协作系统中的操作”的问题。 它建议撤消管理器从应用程序中获取“冲突（A，B）”回调，具有以下规范（请参阅第 4.2.1 节）：

如果按顺序执行的相邻操作 A 和 B 无法重新排序，则应用程序提供的 Conflict(A, B) 函数必须返回 true，否则返回 false。 冲突概念的重要性在于它对操作 A 和 B 施加了顺序。 如果 Conflict(A, B) 为 true，则通常不能在不影响结果的情况下更改操作 A 和 B 的顺序。 此外，一般情况下，操作A无法撤消，除非撤消下面的操作B

然后，本文提供了有关用户意图的见解（请参阅第 5 节“选择性撤消算法”）：

如果操作 A 被撤消，我们假设用户希望他们的文档进入如果操作 A 从未执行但所有其他操作都已执行的情况下它会进入的状态

为了实现这一点，所提出的算法首先回滚我们想要撤消的操作之后发生的所有内容，制作“未来”堆栈的备份副本，并尝试通过“冒泡”我们试图摆脱堆栈的操作来执行撤消，有点像冒泡排序。 在每个步骤中，它都会检查我们要撤消的操作 (A) 是否与下一个相邻操作 (B) 冲突。 如果没有，它们可以交换，我们可以执行 B 的“转置”版本而不执行 A。 应用程序需要提供的这个“transpose(A,B)”函数在文本编辑的上下文中有意义，例如，如果操作 A 从未发生过，光标位置可能会有所不同。 该算法继续在堆栈中向上工作，直到到达顶部（成功）或遇到冲突。 如果遇到冲突，它会通过检查“future”是否有相反的操作来尝试消除冲突；如果是，则两者都可以安全地移除。 如果无法消除冲突，则算法确定操作无法撤消（失败）。 当发生这种情况时，本文提供了两种选择（参见第 8.1.4 节）：

  1. 向用户显示冲突并要求他们解决。
  2. 告诉用户冲突，忽略该撤消操作，并允许用户撤消旧操作。

虽然我喜欢这个总体想法，但我对这个算法有一些问题：

  1. 对于通用撤消管理器，除了协作文本编辑（现在大多数应用程序都使用 CRDT）之外，期望应用程序提供转置函数似乎有些过分，转置函数必须满足五个数学属性（请参阅论文中的第 4.2.2 节）。
  2. 我不希望用户能够尝试撤消某些操作并最终失败。 我想提前检测冲突 - 为了更好的用户体验。
  3. 虽然我认为跳过不良操作是有意义的，但我不确定要求用户对此采取措施是否是个好主意。 如果我们想要的话，我们应该实现版本历史或版本控制等功能，而不是撤消/重做。 一般来说，让用户了解情况是一个好主意，但我们应该渴望以一种不造成干扰的方式做到这一点。

处理冲突 - 撤消管理者视角（实践）

考虑到所有这些，我最终得到了以下实现：撤消管理器允许每个条目（操作）具有属性“scopeName”、“hasUndoConflict”和“hasRedoConflict”。 与论文中的“冲突（A，B）”函数不同，该函数需要两个相邻的操作，我的函数检查单个撤消或重做操作在应用程序当前状态的上下文中是否有效。

每次操作后，冲突检查都会在撤消和重做堆栈的“头部”运行，并删除冲突条目（以及具有相同作用域名称的所有其他条目），直到找到不冲突的条目。 这样，用户可以采取的下一个操作始终是不冲突的。 撤消管理器提供了一种方法来告诉用户何时删除冲突的条目（通过“更改原因”），但在演示应用程序中我以一种非常微妙的方式使用它。

总而言之，这是单个撤消重做条目的类型定义：

export type UndoEntry = {
    operation: () => void;
    reverseOperation: () => void;
    hasUndoConflict?: () => boolean | Promise<boolean>;
    hasRedoConflict?: () => boolean | Promise<boolean>;
    // determines what gets removed when there are conflicts
    scopeName: string;
    // will be returned from subscribeToCanUndoRedoChange so you can display it in a tooltip next to the buttons (e.g "un-create item")
    description: string;
    reverseDescription: string;
};

处理冲突 - 应用程序视角

因此，撤消管理器提供了一种处理冲突的方法，但由应用程序提供实际的冲突检查逻辑。 这件事该怎么办呢？ 一个有用的概念是“所有权”。

在单用户应用程序中，不存在谁拥有数据的问题 - 只有一个用户，但多用户协作应用程序又如何呢？ 我们可以这样想：最后修改一条数据（直接修改 - 不是通过撤消或重做）的用户拥有它。 数据的所有者可以安全地撤消/重做对其所做的更改，而无需覆盖其他人的更改。 例如，如果我创建了一个待办事项，而您修改了其描述，我应该无法撤消该项目的创建，但我仍然应该能够撤消撤消堆栈中的任何其他内容。 所有权的粒度由应用程序决定。 如果我修改了某个项目的文本，然后您将其标记为已完成，那么我可能可以撤消我的更改，因为我拥有描述，而您拥有完整性。 如果我后来直接修改完整性，我应该能够撤消和重做，但你不应该，因为我接管了完整性。

获得正确的用户体验

在上面的 gif 中，您是否注意到了一个小工具提示（在本演示中只是一个“标题”属性），它告诉用户当他们将鼠标悬停在按钮上时单击撤消/重做时会发生什么？ 您是否注意到当撤消/重做堆栈发生变化时按钮的动画效果如何？ 为了实现这些，undo-manager 提供了一个简单的发布-订阅服务，以便消费者可以跟上进度。

处理异步

撤消管理器必须能够处理同步和异步操作，因为所有 Replicache 调用都是异步的，并且在其他现实系统中，对后端或外部 API 的任何调用也将是异步的。 异步操作的挑战在于，它们可以按照与启动方式不同的顺序完成（取决于每个承诺需要多长时间才能解决），并在“状态之间”查询系统。 例如，一个操作开始运行，然后在等待某些操作时，“撤消”或冲突检查开始运行并进行自己的更改。 为了解决这个问题，我引入了一个简单的模块，它使用队列串行执行异步操作。

我的演示实施不足的地方

如果您读过我之前的文章，您就会知道 Replicache 给我留下了深刻的印象。 这仍然是事实，但在向应用程序添加撤消重做时，我遇到了一些障碍（缺少功能）。 值得注意的是，撤消管理器本身是通用的（与 Replicache 无关），但确实提出了一些 Replicache 无法满足的期望（所有这些似乎都是可以修复的）。 以下是我面临的主要挑战：

  1. 区分自身更新和外部更新：当 Replicache 通知应用程序有关来自服务器的传入更改时，它并不指示这些更改是源自当前会话还是某个其他会话（外部）。 我们希望在有传入的外部更改时启动冲突检查，否则它们在采取操作时（在将其发送到服务器之前）已经运行，但是如何呢？ 我最终添加了一些特定于应用程序的逻辑来检测这一点。 理想情况下，一旦 Replicache 公开该信息（此处的相关问题），就不需要这种黑客攻击。
  2. 乐观更新失败：Replicache 使用乐观更新，这意味着服务器可以拒绝操作或返回与预期结果不同的结果。 当发生这种情况时，状态将回滚并调整以反映服务器状态。 当 Replicache 执行此操作时，它不会通知应用程序，而是作为任何其他状态更新进入。 这使得调整撤消堆栈变得困难，其中仍然包含服务器刚刚拒绝的原始更新。 我本来可以解决这个问题，但选择在这个 POC 中不实现它。 理想情况下，Replicache 将来会公开该信息。
  3. 从离线模式返回：如果您离线，您可以执行任何您想做的操作（包括撤消/重做），当您重新上线时，您的更改将被推送到服务器并覆盖其他用户在您离线时所做的任何操作。 此问题并非特定于撤消/重做，而是我的应用程序使用的“最后写入获胜”冲突解决策略的结果。 理论上，可以通过向服务器的变异器添加更复杂的逻辑来缓解这种情况，但这需要更多的研究才能正确（也许是另一篇文章的好主题）。
  4. 缺乏与基于 CRDT 的撤消集成：以用户友好的方式支持嵌入式文本编辑器仍然是一个挑战（我还没有尝试过，这是未来帖子的另一个想法:)）。

结束语

我们在这篇文章中介绍了很多内容。 虽然我大部分时间都在讨论撤消管理器的不同方面，但实际上我的大部分时间和精力都花在仔细思考和实现应用程序的反向操作和冲突检查逻辑上。

在某些情况下，我必须重构应用程序并分解操作以使它们易于撤消/重做。 例如，“completeAllItems”不能仍然是一个使用每个 item-id 调用“updateItem”的简单循环；它必须成为具有自己的反向逻辑的自己的东西（因为可能另一个用户添加或编辑了项目）。 还需要对后端进行一些更改，例如添加“取消删除”操作，这与“创建”不同，因为它保留了项目的原始排序位置。 数据库架构发生了变化，因为我需要在每个待办事项上添加一个“updatedBy”字段，这些只是一些示例。 当您的应用程序具有撤消重做功能时，测试是另一项会大幅增长的任务。

换句话说，撤消重做是使应用程序中的所有其他功能的实现和维护变得更加复杂和耗时的功能之一。 值得吗？ 我认为对于任何类型的生产力应用程序和内容编辑器来说，答案都是肯定的，但您需要知道自己要做什么。 这绝对不适合胆小的人。
